title: A Young Person's Independence: Boundaries in Relationships and Mature Filial Piety
summary:
When your son, between the ages of sixteen and eighteen, begins to make decisions about his studies, time, and friends, a hidden fear might creep into your heart: "Has he distanced himself from me? Is his independence a sign of weakened filial piety?" This concern is very understandable, but confusing healthy independence with disobedience is the quickest way to a conflict that exhausts both parties.

In truth, a young person's maturity and independence of opinion are the fruit of your successful upbringing, not a sign of its failure! Your role at this stage transforms from the "manager" who decides every detail to the "wise advisor" who engages in dialogue, explains consequences, and then leaves room for decisions where there is no religious prohibition or severe harm. The Prophet ﷺ said: "Religion is sincerity" (Sahih Muslim — Hadith 55). Sincere advice is offered with gentleness, respect, and kind words: ﴿وَقُل لِّعِبَادِي يَقُولُوا الَّتِي هِيَ أَحْسَنُ﴾ (interpretation of the meaning: "And tell My servants to say that which is best" — Surah Al-Isra 17:53).

When you respect your young person's opinion, consult them, and distinguish between uncompromisable principles and personal preferences where people differ, their adherence to honoring you and their appreciation for your opinion will increase. This is because they return to you by their choice and love, not out of fear or coercion. Balanced independence and sincere filial piety are not adversaries; rather, they are two wings that carry your young person to maturity.
try_this: Tonight: Open a calm conversation with your son or daughter – unrelated to a current problem – in which you ask them about their vision for something related to their academic year or their upcoming plan, and listen to the end of their words before expressing your opinion.
